sections.title: Timing
sections.content: Season: Fall (Autumn). Month: October or November. Dates: Varies according to the Hindu lunar calendar.

sections.title: Regions
sections.content: Celebrated widely across all of India.

sections.title: Significance
sections.content: Diwali symbolizes the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. Associated primarily with the story of Lord Rama's return to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile and his victory over the demon king Ravana. To celebrate his return, the people lit oil lamps (diyas), hence the tradition of lighting lamps.

sections.title: Celebration Customs
sections.content: Lighting lamps and Candles: Homes and streets decorated with clay lamps, candles, and electric lights. Fireworks and Crackers: Symbolizing joy and celebrating the triumph of good. Rangoli Creation: Colorful decorative patterns made on floors, using colored powders, rice, flowers, or sand. Exchanging Gifts: Friends and family exchange sweets, dry fruits, and other gifts symbolizing goodwill.

sections.title: Traditional Attire
sections.content: Women wear sarees. Men wear traditional kurtas & Pyjamas.

harvest_festival.name: Harvest Festival
harvest_festival.description: Makar Sankranti / Uttarayan / Pongal / Magh Bihu / Lohri

sections.title: Other Names & Regions
sections.content: Uttarayan (aka Makar Sankranti): North, West & Central India. Pongal: South India. Magh Bihu (aka Bhogali Bihu): East India. Lohri: North India.

sections.title: Timing
sections.content: Season: Winter. Month: January (Winter Solstice). Dates: January 13-15 annually. 13 Jan: Lohri - Evening bonfires in North. 14 Jan: Makar Sankranti/Pongal - Kite flying in West, cooking sweet rice in South. 15 Jan: Magh Bihu/Makar Sankranti/Pongal - Cultural performances & games in East, Day 2 of kite flying in West, cattle celebration in South.

sections.title: Significance
sections.content: Celebrates harvest season and gratitude to nature. Marks the sun's movement northward, signifying warmer and longer days ahead.

sections.title: Celebration Customs
sections.content: Makar Sankranti/Uttarayan: Kite flying competitions. Pongal: Special preparation of sweet rice dish ('Pongal'), decorated cows honored and worshipped. Magh Bihu: Traditional games like buffalo fights and cultural performances. Lohri: Evening bonfires with singing and dancing.

options: Celebrate the end of harvest season

sections.title: Timing
sections.content: Season: Spring. Month: March. Dates: Varies according to Hindu lunar calendar.

sections.title: Regions
sections.content: Celebrated across whole India - North, West, South, East, and Central regions.

sections.title: Significance
sections.content: Celebrates the arrival of spring, symbolizing renewal and rebirth. Holi also signifies unity, friendship, and social harmony.

sections.title: Celebration Customs
sections.content: Color Play: Throwing vibrant colored powders and water balloons. Music & Dance: Singing traditional folk songs, dancing, playing drums. Social Gatherings: Friends, family, and communities unite in celebration, overcoming social barriers.

sections.title: Fun Fact
sections.content: This is the only festival where you have to wear old clothes due to staining from colors.
